headline: Boston’s Fairmount Apartments to receive more than $16 million in upgrades
dek: The Hyde Park public-housing community will get accessibility, cooling, electrification and stormwater improvements, but the renovation schedule has not yet been announced.
body: More than $16 million in public money will fund the first phase of a long-term modernization effort at Fairmount Apartments, a public-housing community in Boston’s Hyde Park. City, state and federal officials announced the investment Wednesday alongside residents, describing a project aimed at preserving existing affordable homes while making them safer, more accessible and better prepared for extreme weather. The [Boston Housing Authority’s announcement](https://www.bostonhousing.org/en/News/City-of-Boston-announces-more-than-%2416-million-to.aspx) places the work inside a broader master-planning process for the property.

The funding package combines three major sources: a $10 million High Leverage Asset Preservation Program grant from the state Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities, $5 million in Boston capital funds and $1 million in federal Community Project Funding secured by U.S. Rep. Ayanna Pressley and Sens. Edward Markey and Elizabeth Warren. The Boston Public Health Commission is also providing money for open-space improvements and community gardens, although the city and BHA did not specify that amount in the announcement. The total therefore covers more than a single building repair contract; it is the initial public investment in a multi-phase plan.

The first construction priorities are closely tied to daily life inside the apartments. The BHA says the work will modernize unit interiors, make 5% of apartments fully accessible, replace fossil-fuel heating and hot-water systems with electric equipment, and add cooling. Building-envelope improvements are also planned. Together, those measures could affect utility use, summer heat exposure and the ability of residents with mobility needs to live in units designed around accessibility, though Wednesday’s announcement did not provide a construction timetable or say which apartments will be addressed first.

The plan also treats the surrounding grounds as part of the housing investment. Green stormwater infrastructure and rain gardens are intended to reduce runoff and help limit flooding and pollution. The work is connected to stormwater projects serving the Fairmount, Gallivan and Franklin Field communities, according to the BHA. Boston’s PowerCorps program will train local residents to build and maintain the rain gardens while earning green-career credentials, giving the project a workforce component as well as an environmental one.

Fairmount was built in 1951 and contains more than 200 units of state public housing, according to the BHA. That history helps explain why the announcement focuses on preservation rather than only on new construction. The city has said it built nearly 16,000 new housing units over the past five years, but Mayor Michelle Wu argued that adding homes does not remove the need to repair and protect the affordable units families already occupy. GBH News, which attended the announcement, reported that residents emphasized the community’s diversity and their sense of safety while officials outlined the upgrades.

The state funding also reflects a policy choice about where affordable-housing dollars go. Secretary of Housing and Livable Communities Juana Matias said the Affordable Homes Act has expanded the state’s ability to invest in public housing, framing Fairmount as an example of rehabilitation alongside new housing production. That distinction matters in Hyde Park, where residents are not waiting for a future development to become available; they live in the existing community that will have to remain usable during a renovation process that has not yet been fully scheduled.

Several practical questions remain open. The public announcement does not identify a start date, completion date, construction phasing plan or temporary relocation policy. It also does not say how the 5% accessibility target will be distributed among the more than 200 apartments. Those details will matter to residents deciding how improvements could affect access to their homes, heating and cooling, parking, common areas and community gardens. The BHA’s next step is the master-planning process, which is intended to set an area-wide vision while the first physical improvements move forward.

For Fairmount families, the significance of the package is its combination of immediate building work and longer-term resilience planning. New cooling and accessible units address conditions inside homes; electrification and envelope work can improve the buildings’ energy performance; and rain gardens address water that moves through the neighborhood. The investment is not a promise that every need at the property has been solved, and officials have not announced a final design or schedule. It is a confirmed first phase that now shifts attention to planning, resident engagement and the details of delivering the work without disrupting the affordable homes it is meant to preserve.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Boston Fairmount Apartments set for $16M modernization
seoDescription: Boston announced more than $16 million for accessibility, cooling, electrification and stormwater improvements at Fairmount Apartments in Hyde Park.
